I have nothing to say about the puzzle. However, I just realized I don't know the Polish word for PESTLE.

The meaning of the name for the bowl of the thing is the same in both our languages - it's "mortar" in English and "moździerz" in Polish. Just like in English, the Polish "moździerz" means both the heavy kitchen bowl for grinding stuff and a type of cannon (and both words share the same, Latin etymology, from "mortarium", a vessel for grinding). Yet we don't really call the pestle anything. Dictionaries say the name for it is "tłuczek", but I've never heard this word used in the context of a mortar before. "Tłuczek" (related to the verb "tłuc", to hit very hard), to me, refers only to a meat tenderizer or potato masher (tłuczek do mięsa/tłuczek do ziemniaków, respectively).

When a Polish person uses a mortar and pestle, they just say they used the mortar (Użyłem moździerza by utrzeć kmin rzymski - I used a mortar [and pestle - this bit is missing in the Polish sentence] to grind cumin).

I also wondered if the name Marsha (which I suppose is a variant of Marcia?) has a Polish equivalent. It does! It is Marcja [Marts-yah], but I've never met a person called that, over here. The name pretty much only comes up in Ancient Roman contexts. We have no direct equivalent of the name Mabel though. However, the names Amanda (extremely rare over here - I've never heard of a Polish Amanda) and Miła (also very rare) have a similar meaning (Loveable).

The long, protean career of IGOR Stravinsky can be divided into several phases--from Russian nationalist romanticism (Firebird), through Russian brutalism (Rite of Spring), and on to neo-classicism (Dunbarton Oaks Concerto, et ALII). But only at the very end of his career did he eschew key signatures altogether, and fully embrace ATONAL music. It's thorny stuff, and not to everyone's taste. Here is his last completed work, for soprano and piano, from 1966--a RACY TALE of a rather unorthodox HONEYMOON: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C6DawDM0bhw (2'40".
